Fed: Mary Daly also says another rate hike is needed, markets expect two by the end of January

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on November 12 and 13 that the US central bank will need to raise its rate further because services inflation is not easing. Markets are betting on a quarter-point hike in December, then another in January [1][2].
On Thursday, November 12, speaking at Stanford University's Institute for Economic Policy Research, Mary Daly said: “My inclination is that further tightening will be needed” [2].

On Friday, November 13, in Las Vegas, she repeated that her “bias” was toward raising the policy rate, targeting services inflation excluding housing, which is “not moving in the right direction” and tends to become entrenched [1].

She says businesses tell her they no longer have room to absorb their rising costs and want to pass them on to customers [1]. She finds household spending “surprisingly resilient” and says she is watching holiday shopping [3].
The Fed raised its rate in September, the first time in three years, then held it in October in a range of 3.75% to 4% [1]; the effective overnight rate was 3.88% on November 11 [6].

On November 10, Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point hike should be considered in December if October's “core” inflation reached 0.3% month on month: that is exactly the figure released a few hours later [4].
Lorie Logan, president of the Dallas Fed, who votes in December, is calling for “at least two more 25 basis point hikes,” or half a point in total before a pause [5].
Markets are betting on a quarter-point hike at each of the next two meetings, on December 8 and 9 and then January 26 and 27; Mary Daly did not side with those who want to move faster or harder [1].

Key takeaway: when Fed officials with different leanings say the same thing, a December hike becomes almost certain. The question is no longer “if” but “by how much”: a quarter or half a point [1][4][5].

The Fed's most closely watched gauge, “core” PCE inflation (excluding energy and food), was still 3.1% year on year in September, far from the 2% target [1]. The Fed is focused above all on services: their prices, driven by wages, come down slowly once established, hence the “sticky” inflation Mary Daly talks about [1].

The mechanism: by raising its rate, the Fed makes credit more expensive, which slows demand and therefore price increases, but also weighs on housing, investment and, eventually, jobs. Hence the importance of the signal from businesses saying they want to pass on their costs [1].

A Fed that raises rates tends to strengthen the dollar against the euro: things paid for in dollars (oil, plane tickets and trips to the United States, imported electronics) may cost a little more. It also pushes up borrowing rates worldwide, which can slow the decline in mortgage rates in France.

Civil servants: Lecornu offers a month of talks on low pay, unions leave “fired up” and the CFDT joins the November 17 strike

On Friday, November 13, at Matignon, Sébastien Lecornu opened a month of consultations on five issues, including low pay, with targeted measures for 1.35 million public employees. No across-the-board increase in the index point. Unions say the offer falls short and the CFDT is joining the strike call for Tuesday, November 17 [1][2].
The Prime Minister met with public sector unions and offered them a month of talks, focused in particular on “raising low salaries” [2].

Five issues are on the table: emergency measures for the lowest salaries, a reform of pay scales, equal pay for women and men, coverage of some transport costs, and protection for employees who are injured or threatened, along with civil servants' neutrality [1][2].
According to the office of David Amiel, Minister of Public Action and Accounts, 1.35 million employees would be covered by the announced measures [1].

The government, however, rules out a uniform increase in the index point, the value used to calculate the salary of all civil servants: a 1% increase would cost €2.4 billion and is “not feasible,” according to the minister's office [1].
A new meeting is planned after the public sector workplace elections, with the aim of achieving progress by mid-December [1][2].

The union coalition left Matignon “fired up” and is maintaining its call for a strike and demonstrations on November 17; the CFDT, which was waiting for this meeting to decide, is joining it [1]. The central demand remains unfreezing the index point [3].
In schools, primary teachers must declare their intention to strike before midnight this Saturday, November 14, the SNUipp-FSU union reminds them [4].

Key takeaway: the government is choosing to target money at the lowest salaries rather than raise everyone's pay, because a 1% index point increase for all would cost €2.4 billion, in the middle of the debate on the 2027 budget [1].

This choice does not resolve the core of the dispute: unions are demanding a general unfreeze for all employees [3]. With the arrival of the CFDT, France's largest union, the union front for November 17 is widening instead of splitting, which raises the risk of a strong turnout in schools, hospitals and government offices [1].
The timeline is tight: the consultations must wrap up by mid-December, just as Parliament has to finalize the state and Social Security budgets, which leaves little room to spend more [1][2].

On Tuesday, November 17, expect closed schools or a minimum childcare service, and disruptions in public services. If you are a public employee at the bottom of the pay scale, the targeted measures could apply to you; if you are higher up, no general increase is planned at this stage.

Tariffs: after the Democratic wave, some Republicans break with Trump and Washington talks again about a deal with Canada

Ten days after midterm elections lost by the Trump camp, his tariffs are wobbling: the Democrats, who will control Congress in January, want to repeal those targeting Canada first, some Republicans are distancing themselves, and negotiator Jamieson Greer confirms recent talks with Ottawa [1][2][3].

In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democrats won Congress, which they will lead starting in January [3]. According to Global News, the trade war against Canada and other partners fueled this “blue wave” [4].
According to CNN's exit poll, two out of three voters believe Trump's tariffs have hurt the US economy [1].

The Democrats have made repealing them a priority as soon as the new Congress is seated in early 2027, starting with the duties on Canadian goods [1][3]. During the campaign, several Republicans had already broken ranks, some calling for specific tariffs to be lifted [1].

On November 12, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer confirmed on CNBC that Washington and Ottawa had discussed a deal in recent days, without setting a deadline: in his view, the substance matters more than the timing [2]. The US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, had mentioned a deal before New Year's [2].

The White House said on November 10 that it was staying the course; Trump's former economic adviser Gary Cohn suggests making protections against China permanent while lifting the tariffs on Canada [5].

Back in February, 219 House members, including Republicans, voted to end the emergency tariffs on Canada [6]. Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer has introduced a bill that would repeal, with refunds, the 12.5% global tariffs and the 50% tariffs on Canada [7].

A major obstacle: the main tariffs, the so-called “232” duties on steel, aluminum and autos, and the 50% duties imposed under “Section 338,” were imposed by executive order; a repeal law would run into a presidential veto, which can only be overridden by a two-thirds majority in each chamber [3].
Key takeaway: Trump's trade war is no longer just opposed by his adversaries, it is becoming an electoral burden for his own camp, which gives Canada leverage it did not have before the vote [1][4].

But nothing will change overnight: the tariffs were imposed by executive order and Trump keeps his veto until the end of his term [3]. The steel and aluminum tariffs, raised to 50%, will be particularly hard to undo, because US unions support them [1].

For Ottawa, this new situation adds to Mark Carney's strategy of reducing dependence on its neighbor: in Dublin on November 12, the Canadian Prime Minister said he expects new European partnerships in the auto industry, as Canada works toward becoming the first “associate member” of the European Union [8].

If the pressure eases between Washington and Ottawa, North American trade will be the first to benefit. For you, the effect is indirect: a Canada that wants to depend less on the United States is turning to Europe (autos, energy, minerals), which could open up opportunities for French companies.

Macron in Cambodia, the first state visit by a French president since Mitterrand in 1993, with economic and defense agreements

Emmanuel Macron is making a state visit to Cambodia from November 14 to 16, alongside the 20th Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh. It is the first by a French president since François Mitterrand in 1993. Agreements on the economy, investment, culture and defense are to be signed, before a stop in Malaysia [1][2][3][4].
Cambodia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the visit on November 9, calling it “historic” [3]. It runs from November 14 to 16 [1].
It coincides with the 20th Francophonie Summit, the organization of French-speaking countries, held in Phnom Penh [4].
Emmanuel Macron is to be received in audience by King Norodom Sihamoni at the Royal Palace, then meet Senate President Hun Sen and Prime Minister Hun Manet [1].
According to the Cambodian statement, agreements covering the economy, investment, culture and defense are to be signed during the visit [2][3].
The French president is also to co-chair with the king, in Siem Reap, the ceremony marking the completion of the restoration of the West Mebon temple, in the Angkor archaeological park [1].
No French president had made a state visit to Cambodia since François Mitterrand in 1993 [4].
The presidential couple then leaves Cambodia on November 16 for two days in Malaysia, until November 17 [4][5].
Key takeaway: France is seeking more influence in Southeast Asia, drawing on its cultural ties with Cambodia, sealed by the Francophonie, to secure economic and military agreements [1][3][4].
The defense component is the most political: a defense agreement with Phnom Penh gives Paris a stronger foothold in a region where part of the Indo-Pacific's strategic balance is at stake [2][3].

The Francophonie also serves as economic leverage: the Phnom Penh summit brings together the leaders of French-speaking countries, and the state visit makes it possible to turn this cultural event into contracts and investment agreements [2][4].
The next stop, in Malaysia, extends this Asian tour, which is taking place while France is shaken at home by the public sector strike planned for November 17 [5].

For you, these agreements could open markets for French companies in Southeast Asia, in investment or defense, and strengthen the place of French in the region. The restoration of Angkor also touches on tourism and heritage, a field where French expertise is recognized.

news.2026-11-14-guatemala-narcos-terrori: Guatemala: Washington designates three drug trafficking clans as “terrorists” to cut the cocaine route to Mexico

On November 13, the United States designated the Guatemalan Lorenzana clan as a foreign terrorist organization and sanctioned the Huistas and the Mendozas as “global terrorists” for supporting Mexico's Sinaloa and Jalisco cartels. President Bernardo Arévalo sees it as the result of his cooperation with Washington [1][2][4].

The State Department added Los Lorenzanas to its list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTO) and to the “Specially Designated Global Terrorists” (SDGT) [1]. It describes them as one of the most powerful clans in the country, responsible for widespread violence against civilians, public officials and the military [1].

The Treasury designated Los Huistas and Los Mendoza as SDGT: according to the department, they handle the receipt, storage and cross-border movement of drugs for the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), and control smuggling routes along the borders with Mexico and Honduras [2][3].

All their assets located in the United States or controlled by Americans are frozen and must be reported to OFAC, the Treasury office in charge of sanctions [3]. Los Huistas had already been sanctioned since March 18, 2022 [3].

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the decision “exposes the links between politically influential Guatemalan criminal organizations and Mexican foreign terrorist organizations” [2]. For Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the United States will not stand idly by while these groups corrupt Guatemala's institutions [1].

The Lorenzanas operate in the east and north of the country, near Honduras; the Huistas in the west, along the Mexican border, with the backing of local politicians and businesspeople; the Mendozas, founded in the 1980s, are one of the oldest clans [5].

Bernardo Arévalo links these designations, which came during the attorney general's visit to Washington, to the security agreements with the United States: in his view, cooperation has strengthened since the public prosecutor's office is no longer “co-opted by corruption” [4]. He did not announce any new Guatemalan measures [6].
The US embassy warns that associates of the Lorenzanas could face criminal prosecution in US courts [7].

Key takeaway: by treating traffickers as terrorists, Washington gives itself much heavier weapons: asset freezes and prosecution of anyone who supports them, which also targets their political and economic networks [2][7].

Guatemala is a key corridor: drugs from South America pass through it before moving up through Mexico to the United States. Washington is now going after the logistics subcontractors of the Mexican cartels, not just the cartels themselves [2][3].

The decision is part of a regional offensive: neighboring Honduras has also just designated the MS-13 and Barrio 18 gangs as terrorist associations, which Marco Rubio welcomed on November 13 when he received the Honduran president [8].

The direct effect on your daily life is small. But these sanctions show how Washington uses the dollar and its financial system as a weapon: any bank or company, including European ones, that did business with these clans would itself be exposed to US sanctions. And the fight against cocaine routes in Central America also matters for Europe, the other major market for this drug.

Hong Kong: the Hang Seng falls below 24,000 points, Chinese tech stocks lose 3% in Nvidia's wake

On Friday, November 13, the Hong Kong stock market fell 1.55%, its third straight decline, to 23,637.60 points. The tech index dropped 3.02%, Alibaba and Tencent more than 3%, while Tokyo, boosted by a weak yen, ended higher [1][2][3][6].
The Hang Seng Index lost 370.95 points (-1.55%) to 23,637.60, below the 24,000-point mark, dragged down by heavy selling in tech and chip stocks [1][2].
The Hang Seng Tech, which groups the large tech companies listed in Hong Kong, fell 3.02% to 3,813.19 points, according to the Xinhua news agency cited by BusinessToday [2].
Alibaba lost 3.46% and Tencent 3%; computer maker Lenovo fell 6.33%, and property developer Longfor 6.43%, the index's worst performer [2][3].
It is the third straight session of losses: on Thursday, the index had already shed 1.26%, dragged down by tech, while only the real estate fund Link REIT rose after its results [5][1].
Analysts cite uncertainty at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's resignation, but also restrictions on advanced chips and regulatory pressure on the tech sector [2][4].
In Tokyo, by contrast, the Nikkei gained about 0.5% to 61,142.35 points and ended its best week since June, boosted by a weak yen that helps exporters [7][8].

Key takeaway: Hong Kong is the main stock market showcase for China's tech giants. When Wall Street has doubts about artificial intelligence (AI), they are the ones that fall the most, while the Tokyo stock market, driven by its exporters, holds up [2][7].

Chinese AI companies depend on US chips, whose exports Washington restricts: every jolt at Nvidia is a reminder of this vulnerability. They are also betting on Chinese chips, whose stock market listings have attracted a lot of money in recent months [2][10][11].
Real estate is not spared: Longfor's drop is a reminder that the crisis among Chinese developers is not over and is still weighing on the index [3].
The gap between Tokyo and Hong Kong shows that money is being selective: investors are holding on to Japanese chipmaking equipment makers, supported by the yen, and trimming Chinese platforms [7][8].

For you, the effect is mostly indirect: “emerging markets” or “Asia” funds sold in French life insurance policies hold a lot of Alibaba and Tencent, and their value fell this week. European companies that sell in China, such as luxury brands, also watch the mood of the Hong Kong stock market. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why Hong Kong reacts so strongly to US tech news

The Hong Kong stock market is where foreign investors can most easily buy shares in Chinese giants such as Alibaba or Tencent. These stocks carry a lot of weight in the Hang Seng Index: when international funds cut back their bets on tech, the whole index falls [1][2]. Chinese artificial intelligence companies are also caught in a squeeze: they need chips that the United States restricts, which makes their future profits more uncertain and therefore more sensitive to the slightest doubt [2]. In Tokyo, the situation is different: a weak yen boosts Japanese exporters' profits, which cushions shocks coming from Wall Street [7][8].

news.2026-11-14-bulgarie-budget-2027-man: Bulgaria: its first budget in the eurozone brings people back onto the streets, Brussels worries about spending

Protests against the draft 2027 budget took place in seven Bulgarian cities, including Sofia in front of the Council of Ministers. Brussels warns that spending is rising twice as fast as it should, and the opposition is talking about a looming “bankruptcy” [2][3].

On November 11, rallies were called in seven cities, including Sofia, in front of the Council of Ministers [2]. According to the organizers, planned incomes are rising less than inflation, and taxes would increase by nearly €2 billion [2].
Asen Vassilev, leader of the opposition party We Continue the Change, sees it as the framework for a “financial collapse” [2].

It is Bulgaria's first budget in the eurozone; Brussels has warned that its spending this year is rising more than twice as fast as EU rules allow [3]. The bill relies on a one-off windfall tax, expected to bring in about €800 million in 2027 [3].

Key takeaway: at the end of 2025, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2026 budget [4]; according to Balkan Insight, the current turnout is much weaker, but anger remains, including over the government's refusal to name Moscow as the likely perpetrator of drone attacks in the Black Sea [1].
Bulgaria is also one of the four countries refusing to fund Ukraine in the next EU budget, at the heart of the standoff with Germany [5].
Bulgaria shares your currency: if a eurozone country lets its spending slip, it is the credibility of the common rules that suffers.

news.2026-11-14-honduras-asfura-rubio-wa: Honduras: President Nasry Asfura received by Marco Rubio, who praises his war on gangs and talks about investment

Honduran President Nasry Asfura met with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington on November 13, according to the US embassy. On the agenda: the fight against cartels and gangs, trade, and the El Niño-related drought [1].

According to the US readout, Marco Rubio praised Asfura's role in the “Shield of the Americas” and the regional coalition against cartels, as well as Honduras' recent designation of the MS-13 and Barrio 18 gangs as terrorist associations [1].
The two leaders discussed increasing bilateral trade and US investment in Honduras [1].
Rubio reaffirmed Washington's support for Hondurans hit by the drought caused by El Niño [1].
An ally of Donald Trump, Asfura took office on January 27, 2026, after defeating TV host Salvador Nasralla with 40.1% of the vote to 39.5% [2].

Key takeaway: Tegucigalpa is aligning clearly with Washington. Asfura has promised to crack down on drug trafficking and the large transnational gangs, and he has said he is considering restoring relations with Taiwan at China's expense [3].
Migration is also at stake: Asfura has asked Donald Trump to restore Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which allowed Hondurans to live and work legally in the United States [3].
Little direct effect for you. But Honduras' choice between Beijing and Taiwan shows that the US-China rivalry is also playing out in the small countries of Central America.
